claim: Creatine (Cr) was detected in synaptic vesicles (SVs) at a level lower than glutamate and gamma-aminobutyric acid but higher than acetylcholine and 5-hydroxytryptamine.
source: We detected creatine (Cr) in synaptic vesicles (SVs) at a level lower than glutamate and gamma-aminobutyric acid but higher than acetylcholine and 5-hydroxytryptamine.
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data from CE-MS analysis showing Cr levels in SVs relative to other neurotransmitters (Figures 1-3).

claim: SV Cr was reduced in mice lacking arginine:glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT).
source: SV Cr was reduced in mice lacking either arginine:glycine amidinotransferase (a Cr synthetase) or SLC6A8, a Cr transporter with mutations among the most common causes of intellectual disability in men.
evidence: Figure 3 shows quantitative data demonstrating reduced Cr in SVs from Agat knockout mice compared to wild-type.

claim: SV Cr was reduced in mice lacking SLC6A8.
source: SV Cr was reduced in mice lacking either arginine:glycine amidinotransferase (a Cr synthetase) or SLC6A8, a Cr transporter with mutations among the most common causes of intellectual disability in men.
evidence: Figure 2 shows quantitative data demonstrating reduced Cr in SVs from Slc6a8 knockout mice compared to wild-type.

claim: Calcium-dependent release of Cr was detected after stimulation in brain slices.
source: Calcium-dependent release of Cr was detected after stimulation in brain slices.
evidence: Figure 5 shows experimental data demonstrating Ca2+-dependent Cr release in response to K+ stimulation in brain slices.

claim: Cr release was reduced in Slc6a8 mutants.
source: Cr release was reduced in Slc6a8 and Agat mutants.
evidence: Figure 5 shows reduced Cr release in brain slices from Slc6a8 knockout mice compared to wild-type.

claim: Cr release was reduced in Agat mutants.
source: Cr release was reduced in Slc6a8 and Agat mutants.
evidence: Figure 6 shows reduced Cr release in brain slices from Agat knockout mice compared to wild-type.

claim: Cr inhibited neocortical pyramidal neurons.
source: Cr inhibited neocortical pyramidal neurons.
evidence: Figure 7 shows electrophysiological recordings demonstrating that 100 μM Cr inhibited firing of pyramidal neurons in the somatosensory cortex.

claim: SLC6A8 was necessary for Cr uptake into synaptosomes.
source: SLC6A8 was necessary for Cr uptake into synaptosomes.
evidence: Figure 8C shows that Cr uptake into synaptosomes was significantly reduced in Slc6a8 knockout mice compared to wild-type.

claim: Cr was taken up into SVs in an ATP-dependent manner.
source: Cr was found by us to be taken up into SVs in an ATP-dependent manner.
evidence: Figure 8D shows that [13C]-Cr uptake into SVs was significantly higher in the presence of ATP compared to absence of ATP.

claim: The amount of Cr in SVs was 3.43 ± 0.40 pmol/μg anti-Syp antibody.
source: Amount of Cr in the SVs was found to be 3.43 ± 0.40 pmol/μg anti-Syp antibody (Figure 1F), which was approximately 2% of Glu, 19% of GABA, 266% of ACh, and 3573% of 5-HT.
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from purified SVs (Figure 1F).

claim: The amount of glutamate in SVs was 171.1 ± 5.4 pmol/μg anti-Syp antibody.
source: The amount of Glu was 171.1 ± 5.4 pmol/μg anti-Syp antibody (n = 10, Figure 1B), approximately 10 times that of GABA (n = 10,17.81 ± 1.47 pmol/μg anti-Syp antibody, Figure 1C).
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from purified SVs (Figure 1B).

claim: The amount of GABA in SVs was 17.81 ± 1.47 pmol/μg anti-Syp antibody.
source: The amount of Glu was 171.1 ± 5.4 pmol/μg anti-Syp antibody (n = 10, Figure 1B), approximately 10 times that of GABA (n = 10,17.81 ± 1.47 pmol/μg anti-Syp antibody, Figure 1C).
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from purified SVs (Figure 1C).

claim: The amount of acetylcholine in SVs was 1.29 ± 0.10 pmol/μg anti-Syp antibody.
source: The amount of ACh was 1.29 ± 0.10 pmol/μg anti-Syp antibody (n = 10, Figure 1D), approximately 0.072 that of GABA.
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from purified SVs (Figure 1D).

claim: The amount of 5-HT in SVs was 0.096 ± 0.017 pmol/μg anti-Syp antibody.
source: The amount of 5-HT was 0.096 ± 0.017 pmol/μg anti-Syp antibody (n = 10, Figure 1E).
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from purified SVs (Figure 1E).

claim: Approximately 1.3–2.15% of neurons in the mouse brain are creatinergic.
source: Assuming that the content of each neurotransmitter in a single SV is similar, extrapolation from the above data would suggest that approximately 1.3–2.15% of neurons in the mouse brain are creatinergic.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relative amounts of neurotransmitters detected in SVs and known proportions of different neuron types.

claim: Purified SVs had an average diameter of 40.44 ± 0.26 nm.
source: Visualization by electronic microscopy (EM) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, left panel) showed that the purified vesicles were homogeneous, with an average diameter of 40.44 ± 0.26 nm (n = 596 particles) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, right panel), consistent with previous descriptions of SVs (Ahmed et al., 2013; Takamori et al., 2006).
evidence: Electron microscopy measurements of purified SVs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Cr storage in SVs is dependent on H+ gradient.
source: Furthermore, in the presence of FCCP or nigericin, SV Cr was reduced to a level comparable to that pulled down by control IgG (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), demonstrating the storage of Cr in SVs was dependent on H+ gradient.
evidence: Pharmacological experiments using FCCP and nigericin to dissipate H+ gradient showed reduced Cr in SVs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).

claim: FCCP significantly reduced the amount of Cr in SVs.
source: FCCP significantly reduced the amount of Cr as well as classical neurotransmitters in SVs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: Pharmacological experiments showing FCCP effect on SV contents (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Nigericin reduced the amount of Cr in SVs.
source: Nigericin, a K+/H+ exchanger which dissipates ΔpH (Qian et al., 2021; Schenck et al., 2009), also reduced the amount of Cr and classical neurotransmitters in SVs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: Pharmacological experiments showing nigericin effect on SV contents (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Cr in SVs from Slc6a8 knockout mice was reduced to approximately 1/3 that of wild-type littermates.
source: While Cr pulled down by IgG was not significantly different between Slc6a8-/Y and Slc6a8+/Y mice, SV Cr purified by the anti-Syp antibody from Slc6a8-/Y was reduced to approximately 1/3 that of the WT (Slc6a8+/Y) littermates (n = 14, Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data comparing SV Cr levels between Slc6a8 knockout and wild-type mice (Figure 2B and C).

claim: Classical neurotransmitters in SVs were not affected by Slc6a8 knockout.
source: The amounts of Glu (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), GABA (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B), ACh (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 3C), and 5-HT (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 3D) in SVs were not different between Slc6a8-/Y and Slc6a8+/Y mice.
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data showing no difference in classical neurotransmitter levels in SVs between genotypes (Figure 2D-G).

claim: Body weights of Slc6a8 knockout mice were reduced.
source: Consistent with previous reports, the body weights of Slc6a8 KO mice were reduced (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, D; Skelton et al., 2011; Duran-Trio et al., 2021; Stockebrand et al., 2018).
evidence: Body weight measurements of Slc6a8 knockout mice compared to wild-type (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, D).

claim: Brain weight was not significantly different between Slc6a8 knockout mice and wild-type mice.
source: Brain weight was not significantly different between Slc6a8 KO mice and WT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, C).
evidence: Brain weight measurements of Slc6a8 knockout mice compared to wild-type (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, C).

claim: Cr in SVs from Agat knockout mice was significantly lower than those from Agat+/+ and Agat+/- mice.
source: Cr was significantly enriched in SVs from all three genotypes compared to the IgG control (+/-). However, the level of Cr from Agat-/- mice was significantly lower than those from Agat+/+ and Agat+/- (n = 10, Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data comparing SV Cr levels among Agat genotypes (Figure 3A and B).

claim: GABA in SVs from Agat knockout mice was decreased by 30% compared to Agat+/+ mice.
source: GABA in SVs from Agat-/- mice was also decreased from Agat+/+ mice by 30%, to an extent less than that of Cr (78.4%).
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data showing GABA reduction in Agat knockout mice (Figure 3D).

claim: Glutamate, acetylcholine, and 5-HT in SVs were not significantly different among Agat+/+, Agat+/-, and Agat-/- mice.
source: Glu (Figure 3C), ACh (Figure 3E), and 5-HT (Figure 3F) were all enriched in SVs (compared to IgG controls) and not significantly different among Agat+/+, Agat+/-, and Agat-/- mice.
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data showing no difference in Glu, ACh, and 5-HT levels among Agat genotypes (Figure 3C, E, F).

claim: Body weight of Agat knockout mice was lower than both Agat+/+ and Agat+/- mice.
source: Body weight (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), but not brain weight (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), of Agat-/- mice was lower than both Agat+/+ and Agat+/- mice, which were similar to Slc6a8 KO mice.
evidence: Body weight measurements of Agat knockout mice compared to other genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).

claim: Brain weight of Agat knockout mice was not different from Agat+/+ and Agat+/- mice.
source: Body weight (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), but not brain weight (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), of Agat-/- mice was lower than both Agat+/+ and Agat+/- mice, which were similar to Slc6a8 KO mice.
evidence: Brain weight measurements of Agat knockout mice compared to other genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).

claim: SLC6A8 is expressed in the olfactory bulb.
source: Slc6a8HA mice showed positive signals in the olfactory bulb (Figure 4B), the piriform cortex (Figure 4C–F), the somatosensory cortex (Figure 4F and G), the ventral posterior thalamus (Figure 4H), the interpeduncular nucleus (Figure 4I), and the pontine nuclei (Figure 4J).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing SLC6A8-HA expression pattern in Slc6a8HA knockin mice (Figure 4B).

claim: SLC6A8 is expressed in the piriform cortex.
source: Slc6a8HA mice showed positive signals in the olfactory bulb (Figure 4B), the piriform cortex (Figure 4C–F), the somatosensory cortex (Figure 4F and G), the ventral posterior thalamus (Figure 4H), the interpeduncular nucleus (Figure 4I), and the pontine nuclei (Figure 4J).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing SLC6A8-HA expression pattern in Slc6a8HA knockin mice (Figure 4C-F).

claim: SLC6A8 is expressed in the somatosensory cortex.
source: Slc6a8HA mice showed positive signals in the olfactory bulb (Figure 4B), the piriform cortex (Figure 4C–F), the somatosensory cortex (Figure 4F and G), the ventral posterior thalamus (Figure 4H), the interpeduncular nucleus (Figure 4I), and the pontine nuclei (Figure 4J).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing SLC6A8-HA expression pattern in Slc6a8HA knockin mice (Figure 4F and G).

claim: SLC6A8 is expressed in the ventral posterior thalamus.
source: Slc6a8HA mice showed positive signals in the olfactory bulb (Figure 4B), the piriform cortex (Figure 4C–F), the somatosensory cortex (Figure 4F and G), the ventral posterior thalamus (Figure 4H), the interpeduncular nucleus (Figure 4I), and the pontine nuclei (Figure 4J).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing SLC6A8-HA expression pattern in Slc6a8HA knockin mice (Figure 4H).

claim: SLC6A8 is expressed in the interpeduncular nucleus.
source: Slc6a8HA mice showed positive signals in the olfactory bulb (Figure 4B), the piriform cortex (Figure 4C–F), the somatosensory cortex (Figure 4F and G), the ventral posterior thalamus (Figure 4H), the interpeduncular nucleus (Figure 4I), and the pontine nuclei (Figure 4J).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing SLC6A8-HA expression pattern in Slc6a8HA knockin mice (Figure 4I).

claim: SLC6A8 is expressed in the pontine nuclei.
source: Slc6a8HA mice showed positive signals in the olfactory bulb (Figure 4B), the piriform cortex (Figure 4C–F), the somatosensory cortex (Figure 4F and G), the ventral posterior thalamus (Figure 4H), the interpeduncular nucleus (Figure 4I), and the pontine nuclei (Figure 4J).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing SLC6A8-HA expression pattern in Slc6a8HA knockin mice (Figure 4J).

claim: Moderate levels of SLC6A8 immunoreactivity were observed in the motor cortex.
source: In addition, moderate levels of immunoreactivity were observed in the motor cortex (Figure 4D–H), the medial habenular nucleus (Figure 4H), the hippocampus (Figure 4H), and the cerebellum (Figure 4K).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing SLC6A8-HA expression pattern in Slc6a8HA knockin mice (Figure 4D-H).

claim: Moderate levels of SLC6A8 immunoreactivity were observed in the medial habenular nucleus.
source: In addition, moderate levels of immunoreactivity were observed in the motor cortex (Figure 4D–H), the medial habenular nucleus (Figure 4H), the hippocampus (Figure 4H), and the cerebellum (Figure 4K).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing SLC6A8-HA expression pattern in Slc6a8HA knockin mice (Figure 4H).

claim: Moderate levels of SLC6A8 immunoreactivity were observed in the hippocampus.
source: In addition, moderate levels of immunoreactivity were observed in the motor cortex (Figure 4D–H), the medial habenular nucleus (Figure 4H), the hippocampus (Figure 4H), and the cerebellum (Figure 4K).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing SLC6A8-HA expression pattern in Slc6a8HA knockin mice (Figure 4H).

claim: Moderate levels of SLC6A8 immunoreactivity were observed in the cerebellum.
source: In addition, moderate levels of immunoreactivity were observed in the motor cortex (Figure 4D–H), the medial habenular nucleus (Figure 4H), the hippocampus (Figure 4H), and the cerebellum (Figure 4K).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing SLC6A8-HA expression pattern in Slc6a8HA knockin mice (Figure 4K).

claim: High extracellular K+ stimulated Ca2+-dependent release of glutamate and GABA in brain slices.
source: For example, high extracellular potassium (K+) stimulated Ca2+-dependent release of Glu, GABA, and other neurotransmitters in brain slices (Hamberger et al., 1979b; Hamberger et al., 1979a; McBride et al., 1983; Nadler et al., 1977; Keith et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and confirmed by the authors' own experiments (Figure 5).

claim: K+ stimulation induced the efflux of glutamate at 0.46 nmol/min in the presence of Ca2+.
source: In the presence of Ca2+, K+ stimulation induced the efflux of Glu, GABA, and Cr at 0.46, 0.33, and 0.086 nmol/min, respectively (n = 7 per group) (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from brain slice release experiments (Figure 5B).

claim: K+ stimulation induced the efflux of GABA at 0.33 nmol/min in the presence of Ca2+.
source: In the presence of Ca2+, K+ stimulation induced the efflux of Glu, GABA, and Cr at 0.46, 0.33, and 0.086 nmol/min, respectively (n = 7 per group) (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from brain slice release experiments (Figure 5C).

claim: K+ stimulation induced the efflux of Cr at 0.086 nmol/min in the presence of Ca2+.
source: In the presence of Ca2+, K+ stimulation induced the efflux of Glu, GABA, and Cr at 0.46, 0.33, and 0.086 nmol/min, respectively (n = 7 per group) (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from brain slice release experiments (Figure 5D).

claim: In the absence of Ca2+, elevated K+ stimulated the release of a small but significant amount of glutamate with efflux rate at 0.056 nmol/min.
source: In the absence of Ca2+, elevated K+ stimulated the release of a small but significant amount of Glu and GABA, with efflux rates at 0.056 nmol/min and 0.066, respectively (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from brain slice release experiments in Ca2+-free conditions (Figure 5E).

claim: In the absence of Ca2+, elevated K+ stimulated the release of a small but significant amount of GABA with efflux rate at 0.066 nmol/min.
source: In the absence of Ca2+, elevated K+ stimulated the release of a small but significant amount of Glu and GABA, with efflux rates at 0.056 nmol/min and 0.066, respectively (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from brain slice release experiments in Ca2+-free conditions (Figure 5F).

claim: In the presence of 2.5 mM Ca2+, elevated K+ augmented the release of glutamate and GABA by 5–6 times compared to absence of Ca2+.
source: In the presence of 2.5 mM Ca2+, elevated K+ further augmented the release of Glu and GABA by 5–6 times, confirming previously reported Ca2+-dependent release of neurotransmitters in response to depolarization (Hamberger et al., 1979b; McBride et al., 1983).
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from brain slice release experiments comparing Ca2+ presence and absence (Figure 5E and F).

claim: Release of Cr in response to K+ stimulation was significantly reduced in Slc6a8 knockout mice compared to wild-type mice.
source: While Glu and GABA were released in slices from Slc6a8 KO (Slc6a8+/Y) mice at levels not significantly different from those of WT mice (Figure 5B and C), release of Cr in response to K+ stimulation was significantly reduced in Slc6a8-/Y mice compared to Slc6a8+/Y mice (Figure 5D).
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data comparing Cr release between Slc6a8 knockout and wild-type mice (Figure 5D).

claim: The basal level of Cr in Slc6a8 knockout mice was lower than that of wild-type mice.
source: The basal level of Cr in Slc6a8 KO mice was lower than that of WT mice.
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from brain slice release experiments (Figure 5D).

claim: K+ stimulation-induced release of Cr persisted after 10 min of washout in Slc6a8 knockout mice.
source: In addition, K+ stimulation-induced release of Cr persisted to some extent even after 10 min of washout (Figure 5D), possibly due to the inability of presynaptic terminals in Slc6a8 KO mice to reuptake Cr in the synaptic cleft (Figure 8).
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data from brain slice release experiments showing persistent Cr levels after washout in Slc6a8 knockout mice (Figure 5D).

claim: Ca2+-dependent release of glutamate and GABA was not affected by Slc6a8 knockout.
source: Experiments with slices from brains of Slc6a8 KO (Slc6a8-/Y) mice showed that Ca2+-dependent release of either Glu or GABA was not affected by the genotype of Slc6a8 (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data comparing glutamate and GABA release between Slc6a8 knockout and wild-type mice (Figure 5E and F).

claim: Ca2+-dependent release of Cr was abolished in Slc6a8 knockout mice.
source: By contrast, Ca2+-dependent release of Cr was abolished in Slc6a8-/Y slices.
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data comparing Cr release in presence and absence of Ca2+ in Slc6a8 knockout mice (Figure 5G).

claim: K+-evoked release of Cr was selectively reduced in Agat knockout mice, but not glutamate or GABA.
source: Knockout of Agat (Figure 6A) selectively reduced K+ evoked release of Cr, but not those of Glu or GABA (n = 5 per group, Figure 6B–D).
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data comparing neurotransmitter release among Agat genotypes (Figure 6B-D).

claim: The efflux rate of Cr in Agat knockout mice was reduced to less than 10% that in Agat+/+ mice.
source: Although K+ stimulation still elicited Cr release from brain slices of Agat+/-, the efflux rate in Agat-/- mice was reduced to less than 10% that in Agat+/+ mice and 20% that in Agat+/-.
evidence: Quantitative CE-MS data comparing Cr release among Agat genotypes (Figure 6B).

claim: 16 out of 51 pyramidal neurons in layer 4/5 of the somatosensory cortex were inhibited by 100 μM creatine.
source: Of the 51 neurons, 16 were inhibited by 100 μM creatine (Figure 7B–F).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings from pyramidal neurons in somatosensory cortex (Figure 7C).

claim: Fewer spikes were evoked in Cr-responsive neurons in response to depolarizing current injections during Cr application.
source: Fewer spikes were evoked in Cr-responsive neurons in response to depolarizing current injections during Cr application (25 pA step, 500 ms) (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing reduced spike numbers during Cr application (Figure 7D-F).

claim: The inhibitory effect of Cr was reversible.
source: The inhibitory effect of Cr was reversible (Figure 7D–F), typically observed within 2–3 min following Cr application (with maximal effect from 2 to 8 min) and disappeared after 10–25 min washout.
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing recovery of neuronal activity after Cr washout (Figure 7D-F).

claim: The rheobase was increased during bath application of Cr in Cr-responsive neurons.
source: The rheobase, defined as the minimal electrical current necessary to elicit an action potential, was increased during bath application of Cr (Figure 7H).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing increased rheobase during Cr application (Figure 7H).

claim: The number of evoked spikes was decreased dramatically during Cr application when a neuron was depolarized with a current of 50 pA above rheobase.
source: When a neuron was depolarized with a current of 50 pA above rheobase, the number of evoked spikes was decreased dramatically during Cr application (Figure 7I).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing reduced spike numbers at near-threshold currents during Cr application (Figure 7I).

claim: Cr mildly inhibited the input resistance in Cr-responsive neurons.
source: Cr also mildly inhibited the input resistance (Figure 7J), slightly hyperpolarized resting membrane potential (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C), or reduced amplitude of afterhyperpolarization (AHP) followed by the first evoked action potential (Figure 7—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing reduced input resistance during Cr application (Figure 7J).

claim: 35 out of 51 pyramidal neurons were not responsive to Cr.
source: The remaining 35 neurons were not responsive to Cr (Figure 7C and G, Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing no effect of Cr on a subset of neurons (Figure 7C and G).

claim: Electrical properties of responsive neurons and unresponsive neurons were not significantly different.
source: In addition, electrical properties of responsive neurons and unresponsive neurons were not significantly different.
evidence: Electrophysiological characterization of neurons showing similar baseline properties (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: SLC6A8-HA was enriched in crude synaptosomal fraction (P2 fraction).
source: Using Slc6a8HA knockin mice and an anti-HA antibody, we found that Slc6a8-HA was present and enriched in crude synaptosomal fraction (P2 fraction in Figure 8A, enrichment score: P2/H = 1.76 ± 0.15, n = 4) and synaptosomal fraction prepared using a discontinuous Ficoll gradient (Sy and 4-Sy fractions in Figure 8A, enrichment score: Sy/H = 2.02 ± 0.14, n = 4).
evidence: Western blot analysis showing SLC6A8-HA enrichment in synaptosomal fractions (Figure 8A).

claim: SLC6A8-HA was enriched in synaptosomal fraction prepared using a discontinuous Ficoll gradient.
source: Using Slc6a8HA knockin mice and an anti-HA antibody, we found that Slc6a8-HA was present and enriched in crude synaptosomal fraction (P2 fraction in Figure 8A, enrichment score: P2/H = 1.76 ± 0.15, n = 4) and synaptosomal fraction prepared using a discontinuous Ficoll gradient (Sy and 4-Sy fractions in Figure 8A, enrichment score: Sy/H = 2.02 ± 0.14, n = 4).
evidence: Western blot analysis showing SLC6A8-HA enrichment in synaptosomal fractions (Figure 8A).

claim: The sizes of synaptosomes from wild-type mice and Slc6a8 knockout mice were similar.
source: The sizes of synaptosomes from WT mice and Slc6a8 knockout mice were similar, with areas of 0.245 ± 0.01 μm2 (n = 302 particles) and 0.247 ± 0.01 μm2 (n = 317 particles), respectively (Figure 8B).
evidence: Electron microscopy measurements of synaptosomes from both genotypes (Figure 8B).

claim: Cr uptake into synaptosomes from wild-type mice was stimulated approximately sevenfold at 37°C compared to 0°C.
source: Cr uptake into synaptosomes from WT mice was stimulated approximately sevenfold at 37°C (Uptake, Figure 8C) compared to 0°C (Ctrl, Figure 8C).
evidence: Radioactive Cr uptake assay in synaptosomes at different temperatures (Figure 8C).

claim: Cr uptake into synaptosomes from Slc6a8 knockout mice was decreased to approximately 1/3 of that of wild-type mice.
source: Cr uptake into synaptosomes from Slc6a8 knockout mice was less than three times compared to its control, and was decreased to approximately 1/3 of that of WT mice (Figure 8C).
evidence: Radioactive Cr uptake assay comparing synaptosomes from Slc6a8 knockout and wild-type mice (Figure 8C).

claim: Significantly more [13C]-Cr was taken up by SVs in the presence of ATP compared to absence of ATP.
source: Significantly more [13C]-Cr were taken up by SVs in the presence of ATP, with about 10.3 pmol [13C]-Cr transported into SVs (1.03 pmol/μg α-Syp or transportation rate of 0.103 pmol/min, n = 11, Figure 8D).
evidence: CE-MS and HPLC-MS data showing ATP-dependent [13C]-Cr uptake into SVs (Figure 8D).

claim: Mutations in SLC6A8 were found in human patients with intellectual disability, delayed language development, epileptic seizures, and autistic-like behaviors.
source: Mutations in SLC6A8 were found in human patients with intellectual disability (ID), delayed language development, epileptic seizures, and autistic-like behaviors (Salomons et al., 2001; Margherita Mancardi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Creatine transporter deficiency (CTD) contributes to approximately 1–2.1% of X-linked mental retardation.
source: CTD contributes to approximately 1–2.1% of X-linked mental retardation (Rosenberg et al., 2004; Newmeyer et al., 2005; Clark et al., 2006; Lion-François et al., 2006; Arias et al., 2007; Puusepp et al., 2010; Cheillan et al., 2012; van de Kamp et al., 2014; Joncquel-Chevalier Curt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple clinical studies.

claim: The estimated carrier frequency of CTD in females is 0.024%.
source: While CTD is highly prevalent in ID males, it is also present in females, with an estimated carrier frequency of 0.024% (DesRoches et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a clinical study.

claim: Slc6a8 knockout mice showed typical symptoms of human CTD patients with early and progressive impairment in learning and memory.
source: Slc6a8 knockout mice (Skelton et al., 2011; Kurosawa et al., 2012; Baroncelli et al., 2016) showed typical symptoms of human CTD patients with early and progressive impairment in learning and memory.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mouse studies.

claim: Mice with brain- and neuronal-specific knockout of Slc6a8 showed deficits in learning and memory without changes in locomotion.
source: Mice with brain- and neuronal-specific knockout of Slc6a8 showed deficits in learning and memory without changes in locomotion caused by peripheral involvement of Slc6a8 (Udobi et al., 2018; Molinaro et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mouse studies.

claim: Deletion of Slc6a8 from dopaminergic neurons in the brain caused hyperactivity.
source: Deletion of Slc6a8 from dopaminergic neurons in the brain caused hyperactivity (Abdulla et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous mouse study.

claim: Creatine deficiency syndromes (CDS) can result from defects in GAMT, AGAT, or SLC6A8.
source: Cr deficiency syndromes (CDS) are inborn errors of Cr metabolism, which can result from defects in one of the three genes: guanidinoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT) (Stöckler et al., 1994), arginine-glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT) (Bianchi et al., 2000; Item et al., 2001), and SLC6A8 (Salomons et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: All three genes causing CDS show brain disorders, indicating the functional importance of Cr in the brain.
source: That they all show brain disorders indicates the functional importance of Cr in the brain (Stockler-Ipsiroglu et al., 2014; Stockler-Ipsiroglu et al., 2015; Khan et al., 2016; Fons and Campistol, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the clinical phenotypes of all three genetic defects, supported by citations.

claim: Classical neurotransmitters are stored in synaptic vesicles.
source: Classic neurotransmitters are stored in synaptic vesicles (SVs) (Fatt and Katz, 1950; Fatt and Katz, 1952; Del Castillo and Katz, 1954; Robertson, 1953; Palade and Palay, 1954; Palay, 1954; De Robertis and Bennett, 1954; De Robertis and Bennett, 1955; del Castillo and Katz, 1956).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple classic citations.

claim: Neurotransmitters are released upon electric stimulation.
source: They are released upon electric stimulation before being degraded enzymatically or taken up into the presynaptic terminal by cytoplasmic transporters and into SVs by vesicular transporters (Axelrod et al., 1959; Radian and Kanner, 1985; Radian et al., 1986; Guastella et al., 1990; Pacholczyk et al., 1991; Blakely et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Most major textbooks list either three or four criteria of a neurotransmitter.
source: Most of the major textbooks list either three (Purves et al., 2001; Purves et al., 2016; Bear et al., 2016) or four (Kandel et al., 2013; Kandel et al., 2021; Siegel and Sapru, 2011) criteria of a neurotransmitter: presence in presynaptic neurons, release upon stimulation, action on postsynaptic neurons, mechanism of removal.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple neuroscience textbooks.

claim: Creatine was discovered in 1832 by Michel-Eugène Chevreul.
source: Cr was discovered in 1832 by Michel-Eugène Chevreul (Chevreul, 1835; Liebig, 1847) and has long been considered as an energy buffer in the muscle and the brain (Wyss and Kaddurah-Daouk, 2000; Brosnan and Brosnan, 2007; Wallimann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is historical information supported by citations.

claim: Creatine has long been considered as an energy buffer in the muscle and the brain.
source: Cr was discovered in 1832 by Michel-Eugène Chevreul (Chevreul, 1835; Liebig, 1847) and has long been considered as an energy buffer in the muscle and the brain (Wyss and Kaddurah-Daouk, 2000; Brosnan and Brosnan, 2007; Wallimann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Half of Cr in a mammalian animal is thought to come from diet and the rest from endogenous synthesis.
source: Half of Cr in a mammalian animal is thought to come from diet and the rest from endogenous synthesis (Braissant et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Most of the endogenous Cr is synthesized in the kidney, the pancreas, and the liver.
source: Although most of the endogenous Cr is synthesized in the kidney, the pancreas, and the liver (Wyss and Kaddurah-Daouk, 2000; Ohtsuki et al., 2002), Cr is also synthesized in the brain (Braissant et al., 2011; Braissant et al., 2001; Braissant et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cr is also synthesized in the brain.
source: Although most of the endogenous Cr is synthesized in the kidney, the pancreas, and the liver (Wyss and Kaddurah-Daouk, 2000; Ohtsuki et al., 2002), Cr is also synthesized in the brain (Braissant et al., 2011; Braissant et al., 2001; Braissant et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SLC6 family members are secondary active transporters relying on electrochemical Na+ or H+ gradients.
source: With 19 members in humans, family 6 (SLC6) are secondary active transporters relying on electrochemical Na+ or H+ gradients (Nelson, 1998; Chen et al., 2004; Höglund et al., 2005; Bröer and Gether, 2012; Iversen, 2006; Bröer, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SLC6 is also known as the neurotransmitter transporter (NTT) family.
source: SLC6 is also known as the neurotransmitter transporter (NTT) family because some members transport neurotransmitters such as GABA (by SLC6A1 or GABA transporter 1, GAT1; SLC6A13 or GAT2; SLC6A11 or GAT3) (Guastella et al., 1992; Clark et al., 1992; Borden et al., 1992; Lopez-Corcuera et al., 1992), NA (by SLC6A2 or NA transporter [NET]) (Pacholczyk et al., 1991), dopamine (by SLC6A3 or DAT) (Giros et al., 1991; Kilty et al., 1991; Shimada et al., 1991), 5-HT (by SLC6A4 or serotonin transporter [SERT]) (Blakely et al., 1991; Hoffman et al., 1991), and glycine (by SLC6A9, or GlyT1; SLC6A5 or GlyT2) (Guastella et al., 1992; Smith et al., 1992; Liu et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Creatine is transported by SLC6A8.
source: Cr is transported by SLC6A8 (also known as CrT, CT1, or CRCT) (Mayser et al., 1992; Guimbal and Kilimann, 1993; Gonzalez and Uhl, 1994; Nash et al., 1994; Schloss et al., 1994; Sora et al., 1994; Barnwell et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: SLC6A8 is expressed in the nervous system where it is mainly in neurons.
source: In addition to peripheral organs and tissues, SLC6A8 is also expressed in the nervous system where it is mainly in neurons (Braissant et al., 2001; Schloss et al., 1994; Happe and Murrin, 1995; Saltarelli et al., 1996; Mak et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: SLC6A8 protein could be found on the plasma membrane of neurons.
source: SLC6A8 protein could be found on the plasma membrane of neurons (Mak et al., 2009; Speer et al., 2004; Lowe et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: 85–90% neurons in the mouse brain were glutamatergic while 10–15% were GABAergic.
source: Also, 85–90% neurons in the mouse brain were glutamatergic while 10–15% were GABAergic (Meyer et al., 2011; Olbrich and Braak, 1985; Tremblay et al., 2016), which can explain our detection of Glu as approximately 10 times that of GABA (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations, used to interpret the authors' data.

claim: Cholinergic neurons represented 0.81% of total number of neurons in the mouse brain.
source: Similarly, cholinergic neurons (5.67 × 105) (Li et al., 2018) represented 0.81% of total number of neurons (approximately 70 million) in the mouse brain (Herculano-Houzel et al., 2006), serotonergic neurons (approximately 26,000) for 0.037% of total neurons (Herculano-Houzel et al., 2006; Ishimura et al., 1988).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations, used to interpret the authors' data.

claim: Serotonergic neurons represented 0.037% of total neurons in the mouse brain.
source: Similarly, cholinergic neurons (5.67 × 105) (Li et al., 2018) represented 0.81% of total number of neurons (approximately 70 million) in the mouse brain (Herculano-Houzel et al., 2006), serotonergic neurons (approximately 26,000) for 0.037% of total neurons (Herculano-Houzel et al., 2006; Ishimura et al., 1988).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations, used to interpret the authors' data.

claim: Classical neurotransmitters are stored in SVs with an acidic environment inside (pH of 5.6–6.4).
source: Classical neurotransmitters are stored in SVs with an acidic environment inside (pH of 5.6–6.4) (Egashira et al., 2016; Mani and Ryan, 2009; Egashira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: AGAT is the enzyme catalyzing the first step in Cr synthesis.
source: AGAT is the enzyme catalyzing the first step in Cr synthesis (Braissant et al., 2001; Guthmiller et al., 1994) and its absence also led to Cr deficiency in the human brain and mental retardation (Bianchi et al., 2000; Item et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Absence of AGAT led to Cr deficiency in the human brain and mental retardation.
source: AGAT is the enzyme catalyzing the first step in Cr synthesis (Braissant et al., 2001; Guthmiller et al., 1994) and its absence also led to Cr deficiency in the human brain and mental retardation (Bianchi et al., 2000; Item et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Medium-sized pyramidal neurons recorded had a membrane capacitance of 114.96 ± 3.92 pF.
source: Medium-sized pyramidal neurons (Figure 7B) with a membrane capacitance (Cm) of 114.96 ± 3.92 pF (n = 51, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A) were recorded.
evidence: Electrophysiological characterization of recorded neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).

claim: There was a single previous report of Ca2+-dependent release of [3H]Cr and endogenous Cr in response to electrical stimulation.
source: There was a single previous report of Ca2+-dependent release of [3H]Cr and endogenous Cr in response to electrical stimulation (Almeida et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Cr uptake from the extracellular space into the cells was reported twice previously.
source: Cr uptake from the extracellular space into the cells was reported twice previously, once with brain slices showing sodium-dependent uptake of [3H]Cr (Almeida et al., 2006) and once with synaptosomes (Peral et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Knockout of the Slc6a8 gene increased excitation of cortical neurons.
source: In a recent report, knockout of the Slc6a8 gene increased excitation of cortical neurons (Ghirardini et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Electrophysiological characterization of pyramidal neurons in the prefrontal cortex found increased evoked firing frequency in Slc6a8 knockout mice.
source: Electrophysiological characterization of pyramidal neurons in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) found increased evoked firing frequency.
evidence: This refers to findings from a cited study (Ghirardini et al., 2023).

claim: Creatine has been reported to improve human mental performance.
source: Cr has been reported to improve human mental performance (Watanabe et al., 2002; Rae et al., 2003; McMorris et al., 2006; McMorris et al., 2007; Rae and Bröer, 2015; Wallimann and Harris, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Creatine has been used as potential treatment in animal models of neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Cr has been used as potential treatment in animal models of neurodegenerative diseases (Andreassen et al., 2001; Andres et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Creatine supplement has been thought to be beneficial for children, pregnant and lactating women, and old people.
source: Cr is known to have effects other than an energy source, and Cr supplement has been thought to be beneficial for children, pregnant and lactating women, and old people (Wallimann et al., 2011; Brosnan and Brosnan, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: AGAT and GAMT are not expressed in the same cells as SLC6A8 in the brain.
source: AGAT is also expressed in the brain, but in cells not expressing SLC6A8 (Braissant and Henry, 2008; Braissant et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Creatine and its precursor are transported between different cells in the nervous system.
source: Cr and its precursor were thought to be transported between different cells in the nervous system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential expression patterns of Cr synthesis enzymes and SLC6A8.

claim: When SLC6A8 was completely missing, Cr treatment was not effective.
source: When SLC6A8 was completely missing, such as in homozygous SLC6A8-deficient patients, Cr treatment was not effective. But if SLC6A8 was partially active, Cr was effective (Dunbar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a clinical study.

claim: Intractable epilepsy in a female with heterozygous SLC6A8 mutation was completely treated by Cr.
source: Intractable epilepsy in a female with heterozygous SLC6A8 mutation was completely treated by Cr (Mercimek-Mahmutoglu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a clinical case report.

claim: The absence of SLC6A8 expression in astrocytes whose endfeet lining microcapillary endothelial cells form the blood–brain barrier indicates that Cr in the brain does not rely on import from the periphery.
source: The absence of SLC6A8 expression in astrocytes whose endfeet lining microcapillary endothelial cells (MCEC) form the blood–brain barrier (BBB) indicates that Cr in the brain does not rely on import from the periphery and is instead mainly synthesized in the brain (Braissant et al., 2011; Braissant et al., 2001; Braissant, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern of SLC6A8, supported by citations.

claim: SLC6A8 functions within the brain to transport Cr and its precursors not as a major contributor of Cr transport across the BBB.
source: SLC6A8 functions within the brain to transport Cr and its precursors not as a major contributor of Cr transport across the BBB.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern of SLC6A8.

claim: SLC6A8 mediates Cr uptake into the presynaptic terminal.
source: It is thought to mediate Cr uptake into the presynaptic terminal based on studies of synaptosomes (Figure 8; Peral et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' data (Figure 8) and citation to a previous study.

claim: SLC6A8 is only found in plasma membrane, not on SVs.
source: At this point, we do not know what is the transporter(s) on the SVs for Cr uptake. SLC6A8 is only found in plasma membrane, not on SVs, and is not a candidate for Cr uptake into SVs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization studies of SLC6A8.
